content: In 2021, the World Health Organization (WHO) introduced updated recommendations for tuberculosis (TB) screening tools among people living with HIV (PLHIV). These tools complement the existing WHO-recommended four-symptom screen and include C-reactive protein testing, chest X-rays, and molecular rapid diagnostic tests. Appropriate diagnostic tests for TB include molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostics, lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assays, sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) microscopy, and sputum culture. WHO has also developed and updated TB definitions and reporting frameworks that integrate HIV data recording and reporting requirements. These guidelines include supplementary HIV data elements for TB monitoring tools, such as unique identifiers (UIDs), clinic ID numbers, antenatal care (ANC) numbers, CD4 cell counts, HIV viral load (VL) results, and antiretroviral (ARV) regimen details. Monitoring HIV among TB patients relies on standardized TB treatment cards, registers, and reports, which are consistent globally, although forms may vary slightly between countries. Countries are increasingly transitioning from paper-based to electronic data systems, such as the District Health Information Software (DHIS-2), to improve data capture and cross-program collaboration. Digital tools like the Prevent TB App can facilitate real-time data collection and integration across TB and HIV programs. Services aimed at reducing the burden of HIV in TB patients include co-trimoxazole preventive therapy (CPT), HIV testing for new and relapse TB patients, and ensuring HIV-positive TB patients are started or maintained on antiretroviral therapy (ART). WHO emphasizes the importance of robust mechanisms for coordinating care, treatment, and patient monitoring between TB and HIV services. Integrated electronic data systems can streamline patient monitoring, capturing information on HIV prevention, diagnosis, and care within TB programs, as well as TB screening and treatment within HIV care programs. Co-located TB and HIV clinics facilitate cross-referral, co-treatment, and data reconciliation, improving patient outcomes and program efficiency. Differentiated service delivery (DSD) models for HIV treatment focus on person-centered care, adapting services to meet the diverse needs of PLHIV while optimizing health system resources. DSD models are categorized into group models managed by healthcare workers, group models managed by clients, individual facility-based models, and individual non-facility-based models. These models aim to simplify and decentralize care, enhance task-sharing, and improve community delivery of services. Monitoring DSD implementation is critical to assess patient outcomes, program efficiency, and opportunities for further adaptation. WHO has established criteria for determining whether a person is successfully established on ART, including receiving ART for at least six months, absence of current illness, good understanding of lifelong adherence, and evidence of treatment success (e.g., suppressed viral load or improved CD4 count). Community support interventions, such as adherence clubs and peer support, have shown benefits in improving retention in HIV care. Task-sharing approaches, where trained community health workers or lay providers dispense ART, are also recommended to enhance service delivery. Patient monitoring systems must be adapted to capture data on DSD models, including ART initiation outside health facilities and community-based interventions. Tracing interventions are essential to identify individuals who disengage from care and support their re-engagement. Facilities should implement procedures to detect missed appointments or ART pick-ups and integrate these into existing tools, such as ART registers and electronic medical records (EMRs). Standardized criteria for tracing, such as missed appointments by more than seven days or lack of ART drugs on hand, can trigger interventions like telephone calls or home visits. Finally, monitoring clinical outcomes among individuals enrolled in DSD models is crucial to evaluate their impact. Surveys on patient and provider satisfaction, as well as cost-effectiveness evaluations, can further enhance the understanding of DSD implementation and its benefits.
